extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, students of poetics/drama, and critics of tragedy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and judging tragic drama (plot, character, spectacle, and audience effect) following Aristotelian poetics and critical commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation of the action of a man neither wholly good nor wholly bad
rubrics_metrics.description: "Tragedies ... which imitate the Action of a Man, who is neither good nor bad; or less wicked than good."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The finest and most perfect tragedies imitate a protagonist who is neither wholly good nor wholly bad — a character whose mixture of virtue and flaw allows the audience to feel pity and fear. Examples cited: many successful ancient tragedies that conform to this idea versus those that do not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principal person falls into misfortune through an involuntary fault
rubrics_metrics.description: "the principal Person falls into his misfortunes by some involuntary fault." (described as a general and inviolable rule)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A central rule: the hero's calamity should stem from an involuntary or unintentional error (hamartia), not from mere vice or contrivance; this elicits pity rather than moral condemnation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy's proper pleasure: produce pity and terror by imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: "That Pleasure is that which by imitation produces Terror and Compassion"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy's aim is a specific emotional pleasure arising from the imitation of action that provokes pity and fear. Works should be shaped to produce those passions rather than general or unrelated pleasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce the terrible and pitiful by the series of incidents (plot), not by spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Terrible and Pitiful may be produced by the show, and the Decoration. They may also be produced by the Series of Incidents, and that is much the better way."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet's responsibility is to craft the plot (series of incidents) so that even a reader or a blind person, who cannot see the spectacle, feels the same terror and compassion. Reliance on scene-decoration or stage effects to create fear is a defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: The fable/plot must be composed so recitation alone moves the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: "the Fable must be composed in such a manner; that he who understands the things which happen, altho' he sees them not, yet tremble at the Recitation of them,"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plotting should rely on causally connected incidents ('master strokes') so that the narrated action itself evokes the intended emotions without visual aids; the plot should be intelligible and moving in spoken or written form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid producing terror/pity by monstrous or supernatural decoration/incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: "Those who don't endeavour to find the Terrible, but the Monstrous in the Decoration ... err much more from the scope of Tragedy."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monstrous or preternatural elements (extravagant stage monsters, unnecessary supernatural spectacle) are contrary to true tragedy; they give the illusion of terror but fail when the work is read and distort art and nature (examples: excesses in Aeschylus and some Euripidean scenes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain probability and necessity in incidents (avoid violating plausibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique that some poets 'often offend against probability and necessity' in management of subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events and connections in the plot should follow from one another plausibly and necessarily; improbable or disjointed incidents undermine the unity and persuasive force of the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and coherence of action: incidents should be introduced of one another
rubrics_metrics.description: "his Incidents are not introduced of one another, and the Action does not generally make one and the same whole,"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The plot must form a single coherent whole: events should causally and organically lead into each other (no loose or foreign episodes), so that the action is unified and intelligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus and spectacle must be relevant to the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism that "his Chorus's are often Foreign to the subject he treats of,"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choral parts and stage spectacle should correspond to and enhance the subject and plot; foreign or irrelevant choruses/spectacle are faults that distract from the action and emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Works should please both the learned and the common audience
rubrics_metrics.description: "Whatever pleases the Learned, and the Ignorant too, is infallibly very Good and Beautiful."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reliable test of excellence is that a tragedy pleases both the educated (who notice craft and subtleties) and the general public; adherence to the rules of art is the way to achieve that broad approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of external disturbances (bad acting or foreign elements) that can spoil a fine piece
rubrics_metrics.description: "If nothing that is Foreign, disturb or spoil the [piece], there wants only one Actor to Act worse ... for that which is well plaid, will seem quite a different thing from what it is, when badly Acted."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even a well-constructed play can fail in performance if acting, staging, or other external elements are poor; the poet should nonetheless strive for a plot that sustains its effect despite performance variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: On double/compound tragedies (double catastrophe): must proceed from same action; generally weaker
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion that a 'double Conformation' (double catastrophe) "ought to proceed from one and the same Action" and that double catastrophes often soften tragic effect and resemble comedy's pleasures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compound endings that reconcile or produce multiple opposite outcomes are allowable only when they arise from the same coherent action; otherwise they risk producing the wrong kind of pleasure (akin to comedy) and undermining tragic impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish tragedy from comedy: avoid mixing sorrowful or bloody representation with comic form
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations such as 'And go off the Stage without one drop of Blood being spilt on either side' and 'Comedy ought never to send the Spectator away uneasy,'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genres have different ends: comedy should avoid genuine sorrow or on-stage blood; tragedy may have off-stage violence but should preserve the distinct emotional aim (pity/terror) and not slide into either trivial comic reconciliation or gratuitous gore.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select subjects that can yield great miseries and affect (rarity and suitability of tragic subjects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements that subjects which have 'done or suffered terrible things' furnish good matter for tragedy and that such subjects are relatively rare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose subjects where the magnitude of events naturally yields strong pity and terror; because truly affecting tragic subjects are rare, poets must exercise care and restraint in selecting and treating them to meet the rules of art.
